questions.question_text: Which of the numbers below cannot be written as a fraction of two integers?

options.why: Took any square root to be impossible to write as a fraction without checking that $169$ is a perfect square, so $\sqrt{169}=13=\frac{13}{1}$.
Treated a recurring decimal as non-repeating; it repeats, so it equals the fraction $\frac{2}{11}$.
Assumed a fraction that gives the decimal $0.875$ stops being a fraction; a fraction of two integers is always rational.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{169}=13=\frac{13}{1}$ and $\frac{7}{8}$ are already fractions of integers.
$0.\overline{18}$ repeats, so it equals $\frac{2}{11}$.
$21$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{21}=4.58257\ldots$ never stops and never repeats.
$\sqrt{21}$ cannot be written as a fraction of two integers, so it is irrational.

questions.question_text:
One of these four numbers is rational.
Which one is it?

options.why: Assumed multiplying $\pi$ by a whole number clears the endless non-repeating digits; $2\pi=6.28318\ldots$ is still irrational.
Took $27$ to be a perfect square because it is a perfect cube; it lies between $25$ and $36$, so the root is irrational.
Assumed a minus sign in front makes a root rational; the sign does not change whether the digits stop or repeat.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{16}=4$, so $3\sqrt{16}=12=\frac{12}{1}$, a fraction of two integers.
$3\sqrt{16}$ is rational.

questions.question_text: Which statement about real numbers is correct?

options.text: Every rational number and every irrational number is a real number.
Only rational numbers are real numbers.
options.why: Believes a number with endless non-repeating digits has no position on the number line, when $\pi$ and $\sqrt{2}$ both do.

options.text: Only numbers that can be written as terminating decimals are real.
options.why: Excludes recurring decimals and irrationals, although both can be marked on the number line.

options.text: A number is real only if it is positive.
options.why: Confuses being real with being positive; negative numbers sit to the left of $0$ on the line.

questions.solution_text:
A real number is any number that can be represented by a point on the number line.
Rational numbers and irrational numbers together fill that line, so both families are real.

questions.question_text: Using a calculator, approximate $\sqrt{8}$ to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Truncated $2.828427\ldots$ after two decimal places instead of rounding up.
Rounded to one decimal place instead of the requested two decimal places.

questions.solution_text:
$\sqrt{8}=2.828427\ldots$.
The third decimal digit is $8$, so round up: $\sqrt{8}\approx2.83$.

Assumed an irrational number cannot be represented by a point on the number line.
Assumed every square root is rational and also excluded it from the real numbers, although all rational numbers are real.

questions.solution_text:
$23$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{23}$ is irrational.
It can be represented by a point on the number line, so it is real.

questions.question_text: Which reason correctly explains why $0.\overline{54}$ is rational?

options.text: It equals the fraction $\frac{6}{11}$, whose numerator and denominator are integers.
It is irrational because its digits never stop.
options.why: Assumed endless digits make a decimal irrational, overlooking that the repeating pattern makes this decimal rational.

options.text: It is rational only because it is smaller than $1$.
options.why: Used size to decide rationality instead of checking whether the number can be written as a fraction of integers.

options.text: It is rational because every decimal is rational.
options.why: Included non-terminating, non-recurring decimals, which are irrational.

questions.solution_text:
$0.\overline{54}$ repeats, so it can be written as a fraction: $0.\overline{54}=\frac{54}{99}=\frac{6}{11}$.
Its numerator and denominator are integers and its denominator is non-zero, so it is rational.

questions.question_text: Which of these numbers is rational?

options.why: Assumed dividing an irrational square root by $2$ makes it rational.
Assumed a square root of an integer is rational even though $29$ is not a perfect square.

options.text: $0.101001000100001\ldots$, with one more zero between successive ones
options.why: Mistook a visible pattern for a recurring decimal; the increasing gaps never repeat a fixed block.

questions.solution_text:
$-\frac{31.5}{9}=-3.5=\frac{-7}{2}$, so it is rational.
$\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$ and $\sqrt{29}$ are irrational, and the decimal with increasing gaps is non-terminating and non-recurring.

questions.question_text: Using a calculator, approximate $\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}$ to $2$ decimal places.

options.why: Calculated and rounded $\sqrt{11}$ instead of its reciprocal.
Calculated and rounded $\frac{1}{11}$, ignoring the square root.
Rounded up because later digits are non-zero instead of using the third decimal digit, which is $1$.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}=0.301511\ldots$.
The third decimal digit is $1$, so round down: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}\approx0.30$.
